method.title: Methodology and validation
method.intro: What each number assumes, where it comes from, and how far it has been checked. Status: planned, integration tested, numerically verified, validated for scope.
method.notRun: Validation has not been run on this server yet.

eph: JPL Horizons, DE441. Topocentric azimuth and elevation for an observer on the lunar surface, airless (no refraction).
hor: Smooth sphere, or a terrain mask computed from NASA LOLA elevation. Always labelled; never swapped silently.
vis: Body centre above the horizon, with the range from full disc to first limb (radius 0.267° Sun, 0.95° Earth).
link: Earth in view: line of sight to Earth's centre. Contact (DSN): Earth in view and at least one DSN 70-m complex sees the Moon at ≥ 10°. No link budget.
time: Metrics per interval between samples, horizon crossings interpolated linearly; step chosen by a convergence test.
scope: Landing safety (slope, rocks, thermal). Results hold for the stated site, period and premises only.

aiItems: Spanish and Portuguese text: AI-assisted translations.
method.limitsIntro: Measured on 2030-07-01 + 30 days, terrain mode. Each result shows the disc range and, where a terrain grid exists, the ±300 m range.
limits: Night lengths are measured in full for nights that overlap the period (series extended by 15 days on each side); fractions and energy use the period only.

Site position: published coordinates are approximate, and real landings can miss their target by hundreds of metres. Within 300 m, Shackleton ridge Sun P10–P90 is 48–73 % (centre 99.8 %); Malapert 0–97 %.
The ±300 m range uses a 100 m grid on a 40 m DEM (~2.5 pixels apart), so it mixes real micro-relief with the DEM's resolution limit.
Sun and Earth discs: values use the body centre. Full disc to first limb: Shackleton Sun 94.3–100 %, Malapert 13.3–30.6 %; Earth ±0.95° moves Earth in view by 4–8 points.
DEM resolution: Shackleton Sun 99.8 % with LOLA 40 m/px vs 91.4 % with 60 m/px (same method and dates; see Validation, “DEM resolution sensitivity”).
Earth in view is the centre of Earth's disc. Contact (DSN) also needs a DSN 70-m complex to see the Moon.
DSN only (3 complexes, ≥ 10°); real missions may also use other networks; no link budget.
Observer 2 m above the surface. At Malapert the skyline forms within 1 km in every direction, so local slope and mast height matter.
IM-2 uses the planned landing point, not the actual touchdown position.
Frames: Horizons and LOLA both use the Moon Mean Earth/polar axis (ME) frame; differences between ephemeris realisations are of the order of metres.
Chandrayaan-3 (69.4°S) is outside the polar LOLA DEMs used here: no terrain horizon.
Checked and negligible: time step 60 → 10 min (≤ 0.02 points), ray sampling (≤ 0.05°), horizon reach 150 → 300 km (≤ 0.19°).
Power: Sun–Moon distance taken as 1 AU; the ±3.4 % yearly change in sunlight is ignored.
Power: no dust and no panel degradation.
Power: no thermal model; heaters belong in the survival load you enter.
Power: the panel is never shadowed by the lander itself.
Power and battery values are illustrative and depend on the inputs shown; they are not any real mission's specification.

pgda.title: Our model ({year}) vs NASA PGDA (18.6 yr)
pgda.intro: Our pipeline over the whole year, terrain mode, margin 0, against NASA PGDA product 69 (Mazarico et al. 2011). PGDA counts a body as visible when any fraction of its disc is up, so the comparison uses our first limb; our disc centre is in brackets. Nothing was tuned to agree.
pgda.ranking: Sun ranking the same: {same}. Ours: {ours}. PGDA: {pgda}.
notes: Ranking of the 5 sites by sunlight is identical to NASA PGDA.

Malapert: the point differs by −10.7 points, but the 300 m medians agree within 4.8 points; NASA's own map changes from 18.8 % to 29.0 % between nearest-pixel and bilinear reading at this point, so the reference itself varies by ~10 points there.
Expected differences: 1 year (2030) vs 18.6 years; 40/60 m DEM vs 60/120 m maps; observer at 2 m vs surface.
At Chandrayaan-3 the PGDA map is 240 m and our model has no terrain there (geometric).

report.title: Scenario report
report.assumptionsText: Visibility of the body centre, with the range from full disc to first limb and, where a terrain grid exists, P10–P90 within 300 m of the site; horizon model as stated per site; coordinates from the cited sources (published coordinates are approximate, and real landings can miss their target by hundreds of metres); Earth in view is geometric line of sight to Earth's centre, not a radio link; not an assessment of landing safety.
report.noAnalysis: No analyst answer attached. Ask the analyst and use “Add to report”.

s1: Your mission's landing date slipped. At the lunar south pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth hides behind it: small changes in date or place change power and contact with Earth.
s2: Site A and site B are compared over the same stay. The panel shows the share of time with sunlight and with Earth in view, from JPL Horizons.
s3: Sky view shows where the Sun and Earth sit against the skyline. With a NASA LOLA terrain mask, mountains can hide the Sun even when it is above the smooth horizon.
s4: Compare shows the original landing against a later one, and searches for the next date that meets your constraints.
s5: The analyst answers in plain language, in your language, using the same calculations. Every number links to the tool call that produced it.

learn.polar: At the poles the Sun never rises high: it circles the horizon once a lunar day (about 29.5 Earth days).
learn.libration: Earth stays almost fixed in the lunar sky, but libration makes it rock a few degrees up and down over about a month. Near the pole that is enough to hide it.
learn.terrain: With no atmosphere, the horizon is just the terrain. A ridge one degree high can block the Sun completely.

faq: Why does Shackleton show 99.8 % sunlight but 48–73 % within 300 m?

The published point sits on top of a narrow ridge. A few hundred metres away the terrain hides the low Sun for longer, so landing precision matters as much as the choice of site. Published coordinates are approximate, and real landings can miss their target by hundreds of metres.
Does Lunar Nav say a site is safe to land?
No. It computes Sun and Earth visibility, contact and an illustrative power budget. Slopes, rocks and thermal conditions are out of scope.
Why can Earth be more visible in terrain mode?
On a high plateau such as IM-2's (about +5.3 km), the real horizon lies below 0° in many directions, so Earth stays in view a little below the flat 0° horizon.
Are the power numbers real mission specifications?
No. They are illustrative: you choose the panel, loads and battery inputs, and the assumptions are listed next to the results.
Where do the numbers come from?
Sun, Earth and Moon positions from JPL Horizons, terrain from NASA LOLA, and DSN antenna positions from the DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook. Every result carries its provenance.

azimuth.title: Azimuth
azimuth.def: Direction along the horizon, measured clockwise from north (0° north, 90° east).
azimuth.example: Sky view shows the skyline height at the Sun's azimuth.

elevation.title: Elevation
elevation.def: Angle of a body above the mathematical horizon (0°). At the lunar south pole the Sun stays within about ±1.5°.
elevation.example: At Shackleton ridge in July 2030 the Sun stays between 0.58° and 1.53°.

horizon-mask.title: Horizon mask (skyline)
horizon-mask.def: Elevation of the real terrain horizon in each direction, computed from NASA LOLA elevation data out to 150 km.

geometric-terrain.title: Geometric vs terrain mode
geometric-terrain.def: Geometric assumes a flat 0° horizon; terrain uses the horizon mask. Terrain can lower or raise visibility.
geometric-terrain.example: In terrain mode IM-2 loses 5.6 points of sunlight but gains 12 points of Earth in view.

dem.title: DEM
dem.def: Digital elevation model: a grid of surface heights. Lunar Nav uses LOLA DEMs at 40 m and 60 m per pixel.

lola.title: LOLA
lola.def: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, which measured the Moon's topography.

horizons.title: JPL Horizons
horizons.def: NASA/JPL service that gives precise positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon for any place and time.

disc-range.title: First limb / centre / full disc
disc-range.def: The Sun counts as visible when its first edge, its centre or its whole disc is above the skyline. The range between them is the disc range.
disc-range.example: Shackleton ridge: 94.3–100 % sunlight from full disc to first limb.

p10-p90.title: P10–P90
p10-p90.def: The range that contains the middle 80 % of values. Here, of the results at grid points within 300 m of the site.

earth-in-view.title: Earth in view
earth-in-view.def: Earth's centre above the local skyline: a direct line of sight.

dsn.title: DSN (Deep Space Network)
dsn.def: NASA's Deep Space Network, with 70 m antennas at Goldstone (USA), Madrid (Spain) and Canberra (Australia). Contact with Earth here means Earth in view AND at least one DSN complex seeing the Moon at 10° or more.
dsn.example: In July 2030 the three complexes together saw the Moon 99.1 % of the time.

longest-dark.title: Longest dark period
longest-dark.def: The longest continuous time without the Sun, among the nights that overlap the analysed period, measured in full (up to 15 days before and after it). “≥” means it may be even longer.

panel-factor.title: Panel factor
panel-factor.def: Share of a panel's rated power produced on average, from the Sun's angle (vertical panel tracking the Sun: cosine of the elevation).

dod.title: Depth of discharge (DoD)
dod.def: Fraction of the battery's capacity that is actually used.
dod.example: With the default 0.8, a 10 kWh battery delivers 8 kWh.

libration.title: Libration
libration.def: The Moon's slight wobble seen from Earth, which makes Earth rise and set over the polar horizon during the month.

set.title: Earthset / sunset
set.def: The time the body goes below the local skyline.

provenance.title: Provenance
provenance.def: The record of where each number came from: source, parameters and version.

validation-status.title: Validation status
validation-status.def: How far a claim has been checked: planned → integration tested → numerically verified → validated for scope.

longest-gap.title: Longest gap without Earth / contact
longest-gap.def: The longest continuous time without Earth in view (or without DSN contact), among the gaps that overlap the analysed period, measured in full. “≥” means it may be even longer.
longest-gap.example: At Shackleton ridge Earth sets for about 12 days at a time, so the gap without contact is set by the Moon's libration, not by the network.

pgda-average.title: Long-term average (PGDA)
pgda-average.def: NASA PGDA's share of time a place sees the Sun (or Earth) over a full 18.6-year lunar cycle, hourly, from LOLA topography (Mazarico et al. 2011). Any fraction of the disc counts. It does not depend on the dates you choose.
pgda-average.example: Shackleton ridge: Sun 72.7 %, Earth 51.9 % (60 m map).

psr.title: Permanently shadowed region (PSR)
psr.def: Ground that never sees any part of the Sun over the 18.6-year cycle, mapped by NASA PGDA. Cold traps where ice may survive; dark for a lander.
psr.example: Within 300 m of Malapert, 20 % of the PGDA pixels are permanent shadow.

who.title: Who it’s for
who.note: The people below are fictional examples.
people: The landing slipped 10 days and she needs a clear answer by tomorrow.
Compare and Charts show what the delay changes in sunlight, Earth contact and battery, with the range for a landing a few hundred metres off.
He wants to show his class why the lunar south pole is so hard, without a physics degree.
Sky view and the guided tour show the Sun skimming the horizon and the terrain blocking it, in plain words.
She needs numbers she can trust and cite in a project.
Every result carries its provenance, and Methodology shows the validation against NASA PGDA.
who.answers: For a site and dates you choose: how much of the time the Sun is up and Earth is in view, when contact with Earth through the Deep Space Network is possible, how long the longest night lasts and what battery it needs, how much a delay or a landing a few hundred metres off changes the picture, and how the model compares with NASA’s long-term maps.

privacy.title: Privacy & Terms
privacy.intro: Lunar Nav collects as little as possible. This page says what is processed, why, with whom, for how long, your rights under Brazil's data protection law (LGPD), and the terms of use.
privacy.contactLink: Contact: open an issue on GitHub
sections: Who is responsible
Lunar Nav is an individual project by Luana Santos (team Lumi Lunar) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
Contact is through the project's GitHub page (link below). Please do not post personal data there; ask for a private channel if you need one.
What data, and why

Your network address (IP): only as a hash made with a secret key, to apply the hourly limits on the AI and voice features. It is never stored in plain text and is deleted after 48 hours. Daily usage counters contain no address.

Questions to the Analyst, with the scenario on screen: sent to Anthropic to generate the answer. Identical questions may be answered from a cache for 90 days; the cache keeps only the answer and its tool calls under a hash of the question, and questions that look like personal data (e-mail, phone, CPF) are not cached.

Voice: a microphone recording is sent to ElevenLabs for transcription and is not stored by Lunar Nav. Answers read aloud are produced by ElevenLabs; the audio of the answer text is cached and contains nothing about you.
The hosting provider may record network addresses in its web server logs for security, under its own retention policy.
With whom (international transfer)

Anthropic (USA) generates the Analyst's answers; ElevenLabs (USA) reads answers aloud and transcribes speech. Sending data to them is an international transfer to the United States; each provider processes it under its own terms and privacy policy.
Nothing is sold or shared with anyone else. Calculation data comes from public NASA/JPL services and needs nothing about you.
Cookies and analytics
No tracking cookies and no analytics.

Only your preferences are kept in your browser (local storage): language, theme, Technical/Learn mode, power-model inputs, and whether you have seen the microphone notice. You can clear them at any time in your browser.
Your rights (LGPD)
You may ask for confirmation that data is processed, access, correction, anonymisation or deletion, information about sharing, and to withdraw consent (LGPD, art. 18).

Lunar Nav keeps nothing that identifies you, so most requests are answered by confirming this. For data held by Anthropic or ElevenLabs, you can also contact them directly. To make a request, use the GitHub contact below.
Terms of use
For education and demonstration only. Provided "as is", without warranty of any kind.
Do not use it for operational mission decisions: results depend on the stated assumptions and are not a mission specification.
Lunar Nav is an independent project and is not endorsed by NASA. Data credits: NASA/JPL (Horizons, LOLA, PGDA, SVS, DSN).
